sources.title: M. Habib and C. Paul, A Survey on Algorithmic Aspects of Modular Decomposition

contents.name: §2.1 Decomposition theorem of partitive families
contents.reason: Partitive families are an abstract set-system decomposition theory covering 2-structures, hypergraphs and matroids; the library has reached none of those, and the graph instance this page needs is proved directly from the module definition instead.

contents.name: Definition 1 (partitive family)
Definition 2 (strong element of a family; the strong element tree)
contents.reason: A strong module is one that overlaps no other module, and the tree of strong modules is the modular decomposition tree; this page builds the single maximal-proper-module layer that Gallai's theorem needs and stops there.

contents.name: Definition 3 (degenerate and prime nodes of the strong element tree)
Theorem 1 [CHM81] (a partitive family is represented by its strong elements)
contents.reason: This is the linear-size representation theorem for abstract partitive families; without the strong-element tree, which this page does not build, the statement has nothing on the page to represent.

contents.name: §2.2 Factoring permutations
contents.reason: Factoring permutations exist to make modular decomposition computable in near-linear time; running time and data structures are an algorithmic subject the library has not reached.

contents.name: Definition 4 (factoring permutation)
contents.reason: A permutation in which every strong element is an interval is a device for the linear-time algorithms of §§5–6, and it presupposes the strong-element tree that this page deliberately does not construct.

contents.name: Lemma 1 (intervals of a factoring permutation form a weakly partitive family)
contents.reason: Weakly partitive families and interval structure belong to the algorithmic development; nothing on this page or in its declared prerequisites mentions an ordering of the vertex set.

contents.name: §2.3 Modules of a graph
splitter of a vertex set; uniform or homogeneous with respect to a vertex
Definition 5 (a module is a set homogeneous with respect to every outside vertex)
Observation 1 (every module containing a set contains each of its splitters)
Lemma 2 [CHM81] (the family of modules of a graph is partitive)
Observation 2 (two disjoint modules are adjacent or non-adjacent)
maximal module with respect to a vertex set
Definition 6 (modular partition, congruence partition, maximal modular partition)
Definition 7 (the quotient graph G/P and the representative graph of a module)
Lemma 3 [Möh85b] (a set of parts is a module of the quotient exactly when its union is a module)
Lemma 4 (nontrivial strong modules of the quotient correspond to nontrivial strong modules of the graph)
contents.reason: The correspondence is what makes the recursive construction of the decomposition tree correct; it is meaningful only once strong modules and that tree are defined, which this page does not do.

contents.name: Theorem 2 (Modular decomposition theorem) [Gal67, CHM81]
the modular decomposition tree MD(G); parallel, series and prime nodes
contents.reason: Iterating the decomposition inside each part gives a tree whose nodes carry the three labels; the recursion is a genuine further construction and the page's remit is the single top-level decomposition and its use in the substitution theorem.

contents.name: §2.4 Prime graphs
the smallest prime graph is the four-vertex path
Lemma 5 [CI98] (in a prime graph on at least four vertices every vertex but at most one lies in an induced P4)
contents.reason: This is a structural theorem about where induced four-vertex paths sit inside a prime graph; the P4 structure of graph classes is the topic of the cographs and perfect-patterns page, which is where the tools to prove it are being built.

contents.name: Lemma 6 [ER90, ST93] (a prime graph on at least five vertices has a prime induced subgraph on one or two fewer vertices)
contents.reason: The vertex-removal theorem is the engine for enumerating the prime graphs on five and six vertices, which is exactly the inventory the small-graph consequences page assembles.

contents.name: Theorem 4 [JO95] (P-connected components and the unique separable component)
contents.reason: P-connectedness refines the structure of prime graphs through their induced four-vertex paths and underpins the P4-sparse and P4-reducible hierarchies, a graph-class taxonomy the library has not begun.

contents.name: §2.5 Totally decomposable graphs
contents.reason: A graph all of whose induced subgraphs on at least four vertices have a nontrivial module is a cograph; cographs have their own page in the reading order, and building them here would duplicate its development.

contents.name: Theorem 5 [Sum73] (the cographs are exactly the P4-free graphs)
contents.reason: Seinsche's characterisation needs the induction that every connected and anticonnected graph contains an induced four-vertex path, which is cograph theory rather than module theory and is the declared content of the cographs page.

contents.name: Lemma 7 (classical properties of cographs)
contents.reason: These are statements about the maximal and minimal modules containing a vertex inside a cograph; they presuppose the cotree, so they belong with the cograph development and not with the general module theory.

contents.name: §2.6 Bibliographic notes
contents.reason: A pointer list to Gallai's original paper, the Möhring-Radermacher survey and the 2-structures book; there is no mathematical statement here to build or to decline on its own merits.

sources.title: M. Chudnovsky, The Erdős–Hajnal Conjecture — A Survey
sources.locator: §1 and §2 in full, PDF pp. 1–4 (through Conjecture 2.3)

contents.name: Conjecture 1.1 (Erdős–Hajnal)
Theorem 1.1 (Erdős–Hajnal: every H-free graph has a homogeneous set of size exp(c sqrt(log n)))
contents.reason: The subexponential general bound is the classical lower bound whose proof and its log-log improvement are the declared subject of the classical-and-loglog page, which sits later in the reading order.

contents.name: Theorem 1.2 (Strong Perfect Graph Theorem)
contents.reason: The forbidden-hole characterisation of perfect graphs is a book-length structural theorem; the library has not built perfect graphs at all, and nothing on this page uses perfection.

contents.name: Theorem 1.3 (a perfect graph has a clique or a stable set of size at least the square root of its order)
contents.reason: The bound follows from the chromatic-stability inequality once perfection is available, and perfect graphs are introduced on the cographs and perfect-patterns page rather than here.

contents.name: Conjecture 1.2 (the perfect-induced-subgraph form of the conjecture)
contents.reason: Restating the conjecture with a single outcome, a large perfect induced subgraph, requires perfect graphs and the equivalence argument that goes with them.

contents.name: §2 Graphs with the Erdős–Hajnal property; Conjecture 2.1
graphs on at most three vertices have the property, via Ramsey and the two-edge path
Theorem 2.1 [Sei74] (a P4-free graph on at least two vertices, or its complement, is disconnected)
contents.reason: Seinsche's theorem is the structural half of the cograph characterisation; proving it here would build the cograph page's core result on a page whose subject is modules and substitution.

contents.name: the substitution operation for graphs
prime graph, defined as a graph not obtained from smaller graphs by substitution
Theorem 2.2 [Alon–Pach–Solymosi] (substitution preserves the Erdős–Hajnal property)
every graph on at most four vertices has the property; the four prime graphs on five vertices
contents.reason: The four-vertex conclusion needs the Erdős–Hajnal property of P4, which comes from Seinsche's theorem or from perfection, neither of which is available at this order; the small-graph page assembles both inventories.

contents.name: Theorem 2.3 (the bull has the Erdős–Hajnal property with exponent 1/4)
contents.reason: Chudnovsky and Safra's proof is a structural analysis of prime bull-free graphs and is the whole content of the bull-free page.

contents.name: the exponent 1/4 for the bull is best possible, by substituting a complement triangle-free graph into a triangle-free graph
contents.reason: The tightness construction rests on Kim's lower bound for the Ramsey number R(3,t), a probabilistic result the library has not built, and it is only meaningful once the bull bound itself is proved.

contents.name: good functions and α-narrow graphs; Conjecture 2.2
contents.reason: Narrowness is the weighted invariant Chudnovsky and Safra induct on; it exists to carry the bull argument and has no consumer before that page.

contents.name: Theorem 2.4 (every bull-free graph is 2-narrow)
contents.reason: This is the quantitative form of the bull theorem and shares its structural proof, so it belongs with it rather than with the general substitution machinery.

contents.name: Theorem 2.5 (narrowness is preserved under substitution)
contents.reason: The narrowness analogue of the substitution theorem is proved by the same bookkeeping but about good functions, which are defined only in the bull development; scaffolding it here would mint that definition with no other use.

contents.name: Theorem 2.6 (graphs with no induced four-edge path and no induced complement of one)
contents.reason: The path-and-antipath class is the declared subject of the pure-pairs page, which also carries Fouquet's structure theorem that this deduction needs.

contents.name: Theorem 2.7 [Fouquet] (prime graphs with no induced four-edge path and no induced complement of one)
contents.reason: Fouquet's classification of the prime members of that class is a structure theorem for a specific hereditary family, not a general fact about primality, and it is used only on the path-and-antipath page.

contents.name: Conjecture 2.3 (a positive constant for every graph H forbidden together with its complement)
contents.reason: This self-complementary weakening of the conjecture has no proof in the literature and no page in the plan claims it; recording it as a remark would state an open problem this page does not use.

sources.title: S. Huang, Y. Ju and Y. Zhou, Erdős-Hajnal beyond the five-vertex path (arXiv:2606.06258v2)

contents.name: §1.2 homogeneous set, nontrivial homogeneous set, and prime graph
the substitution operation, given by its four adjacency clauses
a graph on at least two vertices is prime exactly when it is not a substitution of two graphs on at least two vertices each
Theorem 1.4 (Alon–Pach–Solymosi)
every graph with at most four vertices satisfies the Erdős-Hajnal property
contents.reason: The step from the substitution theorem to all four-vertex graphs still needs the property for P4 itself, which this page cannot supply without cograph theory; the small-graph page owns that inventory.

contents.name: the four prime five-vertex graphs: the bull, C5, P5 and the complement of P5
contents.reason: Enumerating the prime graphs on five vertices is a finite classification whose only consumer is the small-graph inventory, and each of the four then routes to its own theorem page.

contents.name: Theorem 1.5 (C5 has the Erdős-Hajnal property)
contents.reason: The five-cycle theorem is proved by a comb-and-blockade recurrence that needs the whole pure-pairs and pattern-graph apparatus, and it has its own page in the reading order.

contents.name: Theorem 1.6 (P5 and its complement have the Erdős-Hajnal property)
contents.reason: Nguyen, Scott and Seymour's iterative sparsification argument is long and self-contained, and the plan gives it a dedicated page after the blockade machinery is built.

contents.name: Theorems 1.7 and 1.8 (leaf and co-leaf preservation, pure pairs)
contents.reason: Leaf-extension results are stated in terms of pure pairs in forests and path-antipath classes, none of which exists at this order in the reading order.

contents.name: Theorem 1.9 (star expansions)
contents.reason: Star expansions of P4 and the C6, C7 and hat-C5 consequences form a separate theorem with its own page and depend on the comb extraction lemmas.

contents.name: Theorems 1.10 and 1.11 (the E-graph and the Bird)
contents.reason: These are the paper's own main results and the terminal deductions of its whole apparatus; the plan routes them to the final page of the extension.

contents.name: §2 Preliminaries: complete, anti-complete, pure and mixed pairs; connected and anti-connected components
c-sparse to a set, and weakly c-sparse pairs
contents.reason: Directional and weak sparsity are the defining notions of the sparse and restricted subgraph page, which is the other pair in this batch and sits at a later order.

contents.name: (ℓ,w)-blockades, blocks, and complete, anti-complete, pure and weakly sparse blockades
contents.reason: A blockade is an ordered sequence of blocks and everything proved about them uses the sparse-restricted vocabulary; the plan gives blockades and combs their own page.

contents.name: (ℓ,w)-combs
contents.reason: Combs pair a blockade with distinguished attachment vertices and are used only from Lemma 2.3 onward, on the page the plan assigns to blockades and combs.

contents.name: §2.1 leaf-reducible and wonderful families; Lemma 2.1 and Lemma 2.2
contents.reason: Wonderfulness is a property of a forbidden family stated in terms of blockades and restricted subgraphs; the plan gives leaf-reducibility and wonderfulness a page of their own.

contents.name: §2.2 Lemma 2.3 (Nguyen–Scott–Seymour: small anti-connected components give a complete blockade)
contents.reason: This lemma produces a complete blockade from a bound on anti-component size, so it cannot be stated before blockades exist.

sources.title: T. Harju, Lecture Notes on Combinatorial Structures in Graph Theory (University of Turku, 2019)
sources.locator: §§1–5 in full — 1 Preliminaries, 2 Clans, 3 Quotients and Homomorphisms, 4 Clan Decomposition, 5 Primitive Graphs; notes pp. 1–31 = PDF pp. 4–34

contents.name: §1.1 Notation: comparable and overlapping sets, families, partitions, transversals, kernels
contents.note: Harju's 'overlap' (intersecting but incomparable) is the exact hypothesis this lemma isolates, and his transversals are what the new lem-the-quotient-is-an-induced-subgraph-on-a-transversal selects.

contents.name: §1.2 Edge coloured graphs: ∆-graphs, the reversibility condition (1.1) and the involution δ on colours
contents.reason: A ∆-graph is a colouring of the ordered non-reflexive pairs by an arbitrary colour set carrying an involution; every statement on this page is about a finite simple undirected graph, and phrasing even the definition of a module in that ambient category would first require the colour set, its involution and the isomorphism relation ψ on colours, none of which the library has and none of which any item here uses.

contents.name: Example 1.2 (undirected graphs, oriented graphs, tournaments and directed graphs as ∆-graphs)
contents.note: Clause (i) — an undirected graph is the {0,1}-graph with both colours symmetric — is the specialisation under which every clan result below reads as a statement about modules, and the remark records it.

contents.name: isomorphism of graphs, and the induced subgraph g[A] as a factor
§2.1 Clans: y →g X, and a clan as a set no outside vertex distinguishes
trivial clans (∅, the domain, the singletons), proper clans and nontrivial clans
primitive and truly primitive graphs; the factor g[X] of a clan
contents.note: Harju's 'primitive' is this page's 'prime'; 'truly primitive' adds |V| ≥ 3, the convention difference recorded in rem-conventions-for-prime-graphs.

contents.name: Lemma 2.1(i) (the intersection of two clans is a clan)
Lemma 2.1(ii) (the union of two clans with a common vertex is a clan)
Lemma 2.1(iii) (X \ Y is a clan whenever Y \ X is nonempty)
Remark 2.1 (the common vertex in Lemma 2.1(ii) is essential: in a truly primitive graph no union of two singletons is a clan)
Corollary 2.1 (for overlapping clans the intersection, the union and the difference are all clans)
Exercise 2.2 (for two vertices there is a unique inclusion-maximal clan containing one and avoiding the other)
contents.note: The proof of the page's lemma runs exactly this argument — the union of a family of proper modules through a common vertex is again one — in the case where the avoided vertex ranges over the complement.

contents.name: Exercise 2.3 (in a symmetric graph the symmetric difference of two intersecting clans is a clan)
Exercise 2.4 (a family of clans linked pairwise by nonempty intersections has a clan as its union)
contents.note: This finite iteration of Lemma 2.1(ii) is the step that turns 'any two proper modules through v have a proper union' into 'the union of all of them is one'.

contents.name: Theorem 2.1 (the clans of a factor g[X] are exactly the clans of g contained in X)
contents.note: The page splits the two inclusions: lem-a-module-of-a-module-is-a-module is the direction that a module of G[M] is a module of G, and lem-a-module-meets-an-induced-subgraph-in-a-module is the restriction direction for arbitrary W.

contents.name: Lemma 2.2 (disjoint clans see each other uniformly: X →g Y)
Example 2.3 and Remark 2.2 (sibas: the axioms (S1)–(S4), that C(g) is a siba, and that every siba is the clan family of some ∆-graph)
contents.reason: A siba is an axiomatisation of a family of subsets closed under intersection, union of meeting members and difference, and the converse representation theorem constructs a ∆-graph realising an arbitrary such family; this is set-system theory over an arbitrary colour set, and the library has no development of partitive or weakly partitive families in which the representation could even be stated.

contents.name: §2.2 Prime clans: P(g), the prime clans, and prime factors
contents.reason: A prime clan is one that overlaps no clan — the strong module — and this page never needs it: Gallai's theorem is reached here through the maximal proper modules of a connected and anticonnected graph, which coincide with the maximal strong modules exactly in that case. Nothing in the 393–442 block is planned to carry the strong-module theory.

contents.name: Lemma 2.3 (a prime clan is comparable with every clan it meets)
contents.reason: The comparability property is the defining convenience of strong modules and is used only to run the strong-module induction; with strong modules themselves deferred, the lemma has no consumer on this page or on any page of the plan.

contents.name: Theorem 2.2 (the prime clans of a factor are the prime clans inside it, together with the factor itself)
contents.reason: This is the restriction law for strong modules, the step that makes the strong-module tree recursive; it is meaningful only once the tree exists, and no planned page builds it.

contents.name: Lemma 2.4 (a minimal clan overlapping a non-prime clan splits into two prime clans)
contents.reason: The splitting lemma manufactures strong modules out of an overlap, and it is the engine of Harju's Lemma 4.4; the route taken on this page reaches the same decomposition from connectivity instead, so the lemma is needed nowhere here and has no destination in the plan.

contents.name: Notes on references for §2 (a clan is Gallai's closed set, and the autonomous, partitive, externally related, condensible and homogeneous sets, the intervals and the modules of the literature)
contents.note: This is the fullest synonym list found in any source read for this pair, and the remark is where the page tells its reader that 'module' and 'homogeneous set' name one notion.

contents.name: §3.1 Quotients: a factorization as a partition of the domain into clans; proper and nontrivial factorizations
the quotient g/X, well defined because disjoint clans see each other uniformly
Example 3.1 (the two trivial factorizations; a graph is primitive exactly when it has only these)
contents.note: For graphs on at least two vertices the absence of a nontrivial factorization is precisely the failure to be a substitution of two graphs on at least two vertices each.

contents.name: Theorem 3.1 (the quotient is isomorphic to the subgraph induced by any transversal of the factorization)
§3.2 Homomorphisms and epimorphisms of ∆-graphs
contents.reason: Harju's homomorphism is a vertex map that reflects and preserves colour equality off its kernel — not the standard graph homomorphism — and the whole of §3.2 is the algebra of that notion. The library has no graph-homomorphism development at all, and the two facts this page needs from §3.2 are proved here directly from the modular partition rather than through a morphism calculus.

contents.name: Remark 3.1 (a homomorphism need not preserve clans; the inclusion of a non-clan is the typical counterexample)
contents.reason: The remark exists to motivate the surjectivity hypothesis in Theorem 3.2, and it is a statement about ∆-graph homomorphisms, which this page does not define; the corresponding caution for modular partitions is carried by the hypothesis of lem-a-union-of-parts-is-a-module-exactly-when-the-index-set-is.

contents.name: Theorem 3.2 (an epimorphism maps clans to clans)
contents.note: Applied to the natural epimorphism onto the quotient this is the direction: a union of parts that is a module of G gives a module of G/P.

contents.name: Theorem 3.3 (the preimage of a clan under a homomorphism is a clan)
contents.note: Applied to the natural epimorphism this is the converse direction: a module of the quotient pulls back to a module of G.

contents.name: Lemma 3.1 (the natural epimorphism κ from a graph onto its quotient)
contents.note: The map sending a vertex to its part is used inside this proof without being named as a morphism.

contents.name: Theorem 3.4 (a set of parts is a clan of the quotient exactly when its union is a clan of the graph; C(g/X) = κ(C(g)))
the decomposition g/X(g[X1],…,g[Xk]) of a graph into its quotient together with its factors
§3.3 Clans and epimorphisms: kernel classes, and Theorem 3.5 (the isomorphism theorem h ≅ g/Ker α)
contents.reason: The isomorphism theorem says every epimorphic image of a ∆-graph is a quotient by the kernel factorization; it is the algebraic packaging of the quotient construction and presupposes the homomorphism notion this page does not build. Every use this page makes of quotients is of one explicitly given modular partition, so no kernel is ever formed.

contents.name: Theorem 3.6 (the homomorphism theorem: an epimorphism factors uniquely through a coarser one)
contents.reason: The factorisation-through property is the universal property of quotients in the ∆-graph morphism category; with no morphisms defined here it has nothing to quantify over, and the uniqueness statement this page actually needs is proved directly at cor-the-modular-partition-with-a-prime-quotient-is-unique.

contents.name: Corollary 3.1 (a graph is a quotient of g exactly when it is an epimorphic image of g)
contents.reason: This identifies two constructions of which this page defines only one; the quotient by a modular partition is given here by an explicit vertex set and adjacency rule, and no epimorphic image ever appears.

contents.name: Theorem 3.7 (a nonempty set is a clan exactly when it is a kernel class of some epimorphism)
contents.reason: The characterisation of modules as kernel classes is an attractive reformulation, but it needs the epimorphism notion; the equivalent working characterisations this page does build are the three criteria of lem-module-criteria.

contents.name: Example 3.4 and Exercise 3.4 (iterated quotients: a quotient of a quotient is a quotient, and eventually a subgraph)
contents.reason: Iterating the quotient inside each part is what produces the modular decomposition tree, and the tree is already deferred to an owner decision in the Habib–Paul harvest for this same page; the single decomposition step is all any item here uses.

contents.name: Lemma 3.2 (prime clans under an epimorphism, in both directions)
contents.reason: Both clauses are about strong modules, whose theory this page does not build; the second clause is also where the singleton exception of Remark 3.3 arises, and it is meaningful only inside the recursive tree construction.

contents.name: Theorem 3.8 (the prime clans of a quotient are the images of the prime clans)
contents.reason: This is the correspondence that lets the strong-module tree of the quotient be read off the tree of the graph; it is the exact statement Habib–Paul's Lemma 4 makes, and it was deferred there for the same reason.

contents.name: Corollary 3.2 (a non-singleton prime clan of the quotient unions to a prime clan of the graph)
contents.reason: The corollary transports strong modules upward through one decomposition step and belongs with the tree construction; nothing on this page forms a strong module in the first place.

contents.name: Theorem 3.9 (an epimorphism onto a truly primitive quotient factors uniquely through every epimorphism of the graph)
contents.reason: The universal property is stated for ∆-graph epimorphisms and is Harju's route to the uniqueness of the primitive quotient; this page reaches that uniqueness by a direct argument on maximal proper modules instead, so the morphism-level statement is not needed and its hypotheses could not even be phrased here.

contents.name: Theorem 3.10 (a graph has at most one factorization whose quotient is truly primitive)
contents.note: The page proves the undirected instance under the hypothesis that the graph is connected and anticonnected, which is exactly where 'truly primitive' (at least three vertices) bites: 3K1 has two different modular partitions whose quotients are edgeless on two vertices, and those quotients are prime but not truly primitive.

contents.name: refinement of factorizations, and Lemma 3.3 (a refinement's quotient maps onto the coarser quotient)
contents.reason: Refinement is the order on factorizations under which maximality is stated, and Lemma 3.3 is a morphism statement about it; this page compares modular partitions only through the maximal proper modules, where the comparison is by inclusion of parts and needs no epimorphism.

contents.name: Theorem 3.11 (the quotient of a proper factorization is primitive exactly when the factorization is maximal)
contents.reason: The equivalence covers the degenerate cases too, where a complete graph on n vertices has 2^{n-1} − 1 maximal factorizations all with primitive two-vertex quotients; that multiplicity is the content of the theorem, and no page of the plan develops the lattice of modular partitions in which it would sit.

contents.name: Notes on references for §3 (the algebraic treatment of quotients, and Gallai's strongly closed sets)
contents.reason: A bibliographic pointer list to Burris–Sankappanavar, Cohn and Buer–Möhring for the general algebra of quotients; it contains no mathematical statement to scaffold, and the one naming fact it carries — Gallai's 'strongly closed set' is the prime clan — belongs with the deferred strong-module theory.

contents.name: §4.1 Maximal prime clans and the family Pmax(g)
contents.note: In a connected and anticonnected graph the maximal proper modules are exactly Harju's maximal prime clans; the page separates the other two cases in Gallai's theorem rather than uniformising them through strong modules.

contents.name: Lemma 4.1 (the maximal prime clans partition the domain, so the quotient by them is defined)
Theorem 4.1 (every clan with at least two elements is the union of the maximal prime clans properly inside it)
contents.reason: The statement builds the strong-module tree one level down inside an arbitrary module, which is the recursive step this page does not take; its hypothesis is about arbitrary clans rather than the whole graph, so even the undirected instance has no consumer here.

contents.name: Remark 4.1 (the maximal clans of a graph need not form a factorization)
§4.2 special graphs (only trivial prime clans), linear graphs, and Example 4.1 (primitive, complete and linear graphs are special)
contents.note: For undirected graphs 'special' means the maximal proper modules are singletons, and the alternatives complete/edgeless/prime are the three cases of Gallai's theorem as this page states it; 'linear' has no undirected instance, since a linear ∆-graph is a total order written in two reverse colours.

contents.name: Theorem 4.2 (the quotient by the maximal prime clans is special)
Exercise 4.1 (a special undirected graph that is neither complete nor discrete has connected graph and connected complement)
contents.note: This is the undirected converse of the case split the page's proof makes before extracting the maximal proper modules.

contents.name: Exercise 4.2 (the clans of a linear graph are its segments; the clans of a complete graph are all subsets)
contents.note: The complete case is the example on the B page, stated there together with its edgeless dual; the linear case is the total-order instance and has no undirected content.

contents.name: Lemma 4.2 (a factor of a special graph is special, and no factor on at least three vertices is primitive)
contents.reason: The lemma is the first step of Harju's classification of special ∆-graphs through the auxiliary graph of two-element clans; this page's route to the same trichotomy runs through connectivity of the graph and of its complement, so no step of it consumes the lemma, and its second clause is false of undirected graphs as stated for arbitrary factors of a prime graph.

contents.name: Lemma 4.3 (every vertex of a special graph lies in a two-element clan)
contents.reason: The doubleton clan is the vertex of the auxiliary graph G(g) in Harju's classification argument; for undirected graphs it says a graph whose maximal proper modules are singletons and which has a nontrivial module has a module of size two, a statement whose only use is inside that argument.

contents.name: Lemma 4.4 (the auxiliary graph of two-element clans of a special graph is complete or a path)
contents.reason: This is the combinatorial heart of the ∆-graph trichotomy, and the path alternative exists to produce the linear case; with the linear case empty for undirected graphs the lemma degenerates, and the page's own proof of Gallai's theorem never forms the auxiliary graph.

contents.name: Theorem 4.3 (a ∆-graph is special exactly when it is complete, linear or truly primitive)
contents.note: The undirected instance — complete, edgeless or prime — is the trichotomy the page's Gallai proof establishes directly from connectivity.

contents.name: Theorem 4.4 (the clan decomposition theorem: the quotient by the maximal prime clans is linear, complete or truly primitive)
Theorem 4.5 (a factorization with a truly primitive quotient is the unique maximal factorization, and equals Pmax)
Example 4.2 (a five-vertex ∆-graph with a linear three-vertex quotient)
contents.reason: The worked decomposition uses five colours and its quotient is linear, so it exhibits precisely the alternative that does not occur for undirected graphs; the B page carries the undirected worked decomposition instead, on a blown-up five-cycle.

contents.name: Exercise 4.3 (if a factorization with at least three parts has a complete, linear or primitive quotient, so does the quotient by the maximal prime clans)
contents.reason: The exercise transports the type of one quotient to the canonical one and is a statement about the lattice of factorizations; the page proves the sharper fact that in the connected and anticonnected case there is only one such partition, and the degenerate cases the exercise covers have no consumer in the plan.

contents.name: Remark 4.2 (the modular decomposition of undirected graphs: parallel, series and neighbourhood factors, components as maximal prime clans, and the primitive quotient when the graph and its complement are connected)
Notes on references for §4 (Gallai 1967 and Ehrenfeucht–Rozenberg 1990 for the theorem, Sabidussi's X-join, Möhring–Radermacher's axiomatic framework)
contents.note: The naming history — X-join for the substitution, closed set for the module — is the material this remark exists to record.

contents.name: §5.1 uniformly non-primitive graphs, and Lemma 5.1 (subgraphs and quotients of a uniformly non-primitive graph are uniformly non-primitive)
contents.reason: A uniformly non-primitive undirected graph is exactly a cograph, and hereditariness under induced subgraphs is the first thing the cograph page must prove; building it here would mean building the cograph characterisation on a page whose subject is the substitution theorem.

contents.name: Lemma 5.2 (uniform non-primitivity, the 2-block property and the doubleton clan property are equivalent)
contents.reason: The three-way equivalence is the structural characterisation of cographs — every induced subgraph splits into two modules, equivalently has a module of size two — and it is the cograph page's central theorem, not a lemma this page consumes.

contents.name: Remark 5.1 (equivalently, every nontrivial subgraph has a proper prime clan whose complement is a clan)
contents.reason: This sharpening of Lemma 5.2 is stated in terms of prime clans, so it needs both the strong-module theory deferred above and the cograph development; it is recorded here so the cograph page inherits the sharper form rather than the plain one.

contents.name: §5.2 Theorem 5.1 (a truly primitive graph has a primitive subgraph on three or four vertices)
contents.reason: For undirected graphs this says every prime graph on at least four vertices contains an induced four-vertex path, since no three-vertex graph is prime; its proof needs Seinsche's theorem, which the Chudnovsky harvest already routes to the cograph page, and splitting the two halves across two pages would be worse than keeping them together.

contents.name: Exercise 5.1 (five equivalent forms of uniform non-primitivity, including the absence of primitive subgraphs on three or four vertices)
contents.reason: The added equivalences are the P4-free characterisation and a condition on the special quotients of every prime clan; both are cograph statements and one of them again needs the strong-module theory.

contents.name: Exercise 5.2 (cographs are the smallest family containing the singletons and closed under disjoint union and complement)
contents.reason: The generative description of cographs is the definition that page will take, and proving its equivalence with P4-freeness is exactly what that page is for.

contents.name: Exercise 5.3 (four equivalent characterisations of cographs: uniform non-primitivity, doubleton clans, disconnection of the graph or its complement, complete special quotients)
contents.reason: The list is the cograph page's statement of its own main theorem; the third clause is Seinsche's theorem and the fourth is stated through strong modules.

contents.name: §5.3 Example 5.2 (the primitive four-vertex graphs: the path, its orientation and its double orientation)
contents.note: The undirected instance is the first of the three; the B page proves it is the only prime four-vertex graph by checking the six connected four-vertex graphs.

contents.name: Lemma 5.3 (a vertex outside a truly primitive subgraph is local or global for it, and the local case has a unique two-element clan)
contents.reason: The local/global dichotomy is the bookkeeping of the vertex-extension theorems, whose only planned consumer is the enumeration of the prime graphs on five and six vertices; the Habib–Paul harvest already routes that theorem there.

contents.name: Lemma 5.4 (the nontrivial clans of a two-vertex extension, for two local vertices and for a global with a local one)
contents.reason: This case analysis exists to prove Theorem 5.2 and is used nowhere else; it travels with the extension theorem to the page that enumerates small prime graphs.

contents.name: Lemma 5.5 (a vertex destroying the local clan of a local vertex leaves a primitive one- or two-vertex extension, or is local at the same attachment)
contents.reason: The last step of the extension argument, and the one that forces the two-vertex extension; it belongs with Theorem 5.2 wherever that is built.

contents.name: Theorem 5.2 (upward hereditary property: a proper truly primitive subgraph of a primitive graph extends to a primitive subgraph by one or two vertices)
contents.reason: The extension theorem is what makes prime graphs enumerable upward from the four-vertex path, and the plan gives that enumeration a page; this page needs only the failure of heredity, which its B companion exhibits with an explicit counterexample.

contents.name: Theorem 5.3 (downward hereditary property: some one or two vertices can be deleted from a truly primitive graph leaving a primitive subgraph)
contents.reason: The deletion form is the one Habib–Paul state as their Lemma 6, already deferred to that page in this same coverage file; recording it twice would be the only alternative to routing it to the same destination.

contents.name: §5.4 critically primitive graphs, and Example 5.3 (a critically primitive tournament; the three four-vertex primitive graphs are critically primitive)
contents.reason: A critically primitive graph is one no single vertex deletion leaves primitive; the notion is the sharp boundary case of the deletion theorem, and no page in the plan studies it — the small-graph page enumerates prime graphs rather than the critical ones.

contents.name: Exercise 5.4 (a critically primitive graph on at least four vertices is covered by few non-primitive subgraphs with a common core)
contents.reason: The covering statement is a structural refinement of critical primitivity, with a bound of three or four on the size of the common intersection; it has no consumer here and no planned page on critical primitivity to hold it.

contents.name: Theorem 5.4 (the parity theorem: a truly primitive subgraph two or more vertices short of the whole extends by two different vertices)
contents.reason: Schmerl and Trotter's parity theorem sharpens the extension theorem from 'one or two vertices' to 'exactly two', and Harju leaves its proof as a hard exercise, so importing it would mean sourcing a proof elsewhere for a statement no page of the plan uses.

contents.name: Exercise 5.5 (a critically primitive undirected graph has an even number of vertices; a critically primitive tournament an odd number)
contents.reason: The parity of critically primitive graphs follows from Theorem 5.4 and shares its fate: the statement is real and checkable, but nothing in the 393–442 block or elsewhere in the plan is about critical primitivity.

contents.name: Corollary 5.1 (a primitive subgraph of a critically primitive graph has the same parity of order, and is itself critically primitive from four vertices on)
contents.reason: The corollary is the usable form of the parity theorem for enumeration, and it inherits both the missing proof and the missing destination of the theorem it comes from.

contents.name: Remark 5.2 (there are only finitely many types of critically primitive graphs)
contents.reason: Bonizzoni's and Schmerl–Trotter's classification is quoted without proof in the notes; a finiteness claim with no proof and no consumer is exactly what must not be imported as a citation-only fact.

contents.name: Example 5.1 (a five-vertex uniformly non-primitive ∆-graph with three colours)
contents.reason: The example is drawn in three colours precisely to show that uniform non-primitivity is not obvious in the coloured setting; its undirected analogue would be a cograph, and the B page already exhibits the cograph-shaped decomposition it would illustrate.

contents.name: Notes on references for §5 (Ehrenfeucht–Rozenberg and Schmerl–Trotter for the hereditary theorems, Engelfriet–Harju–Proskurowski–Rozenberg for uniform non-primitivity, Wolk, Gallai, Kelly and Seinsche for the undirected case)
contents.reason: A bibliographic list attributing the section's theorems; it carries no statement of its own, and each theorem it attributes is dispositioned individually above.

contents.name: Theorem 2.3.5 (the (6,3)-theorem)
contents.reason: Ruzsa and Szemerédi's (6,3)-theorem is a hypergraph statement about triple systems and belongs to the additive-combinatorics development rather than to the sparse-restricted subgraph theory built here.

sources.title: M. Chudnovsky, A. Scott, P. Seymour and S. Spirkl, Strengthening Rödl's theorem

contents.name: weakly ε-restricted and ε-restricted vertex sets, defined by edge count and by maximum degree
1.1 Theorem (Rödl, in the weakly restricted form)
every ε-restricted set is weakly ε/2-restricted, and every weakly ε/2-restricted set has a subset of at least half its size that is ε-restricted
1.2 Theorem (Rödl, in the maximum-degree form)
Fox and Sudakov's proof of 1.2 without the regularity lemma, with much better constants
contents.reason: Their argument replaces the regularity lemma by a Graham–Rödl–Ruciński-type lemma that the library does not have; it is a genuinely different second route to a theorem this page already proves.

contents.name: 1.3 Theorem (a bounded partition of an H-free graph into weakly ε-restricted subsets)
the proof of 1.3: apply 1.1 repeatedly and add the remaining vertices to the largest part
Nikiforov's strengthening of 1.3
contents.reason: Nikiforov strengthens the weak partition to an equitable one in which every part is sparse or dense; that equitability is exactly what the repeated-extraction argument cannot deliver.

contents.name: 1.4 Theorem (a bounded partition into ε-restricted subsets)
contents.reason: This is the paper's main theorem and it is significantly harder than 1.3; its proof goes through statement 1.5 and imports a result from a companion paper, so it is a development in its own right rather than a corollary of anything here.

contents.name: the intermediate statement that V(G) is a union of boundedly many, not necessarily disjoint, ε-restricted subsets
contents.reason: The authors record that this middle statement is not known to be easy and does not appear to imply 1.4; stating it here would put an open question on a page whose items all carry proofs.

contents.name: sets of cardinality at most two are always ε-restricted, and the large star shows parts that small are sometimes necessary
B is ε-sparse to A, and B is ε-dense to A, for disjoint vertex sets
1.5 Theorem (the partition statement through which 1.4 is proved)
contents.reason: It asks for a partition in which each part is additionally sparse or dense to almost every other part, a blockade-flavoured conclusion whose statement needs vocabulary the plan places on the blockades page.

sources.title: D. Conlon, J. Fox and B. Sudakov, Recent developments in graph Ramsey theory
sources.locator: §3.3 The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture, in full, PDF pp. 23–27

contents.name: Conjecture 3.10 (the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture)
almost all graphs have no clique or independent set of order 2 log n
the conjecture holds when H is a clique or an independent set
Alon, Pach and Solymosi: the conjecture is preserved by blowing up a vertex of H1 into a copy of H2
the conjecture holds for all graphs on at most four vertices, P4 being handled by perfection
contents.reason: The four-vertex case needs the substitution theorem together with the Erdős–Hajnal property of P4; the substitution half is on the companion page of this batch and the P4 half needs perfect graphs.

contents.name: Theorem 3.11 (Erdős–Hajnal: a homogeneous set of order exp(c sqrt(log n)))
contents.reason: The classical subexponential bound is proved by the candidate-set iteration and is the declared content of the classical and log-log bounds page.

contents.name: Fox–Sudakov off-diagonal generalisation by dependent random choice
contents.reason: The off-diagonal form trades clique size against stable-set size and is proved by dependent random choice, a method the library has not built and which no item on this page uses.

contents.name: Promel–Rödl theorem on universality versus an unusually large homogeneous set
contents.reason: Universality for all small graphs is a different dichotomy from the sparse-dense one proved here, and its statement quantifies over every graph on c log n vertices at once.

contents.name: the Erdős–Hajnal property for a hereditary family; the equivalence with the single-graph conjecture
the strong Erdős–Hajnal property, and that it implies the Erdős–Hajnal property
contents.reason: The strong property asks for a linear complete or anticomplete bipartite pair, which is a pure-pair statement rather than a restricted-set statement, and the plan builds pure pairs on their own page.

contents.name: families of graphs excluding a path and its complement have the strong property
contents.reason: Bousquet, Lagoutte and Thomassé's theorem is about the path-antipath class specifically and uses its structure, not the regularity method used on this page.

contents.name: intersection graphs of convex sets, semi-algebraic graphs and string graphs
contents.reason: These are geometric intersection classes whose analysis needs plane curves, semi-algebraic sets and bounded description complexity; the library has no discrete-geometry track to state them in.

contents.name: Erdős, Hajnal and Pach: the bipartite analogue giving a complete or empty bipartite pair of polynomial size
contents.reason: The bipartite analogue produces two disjoint sets forming a pure pair, which is a different conclusion from a single restricted set and is the subject of the pure-pairs page.

contents.name: Rödl's theorem: an induced-H-free graph has a linear-size induced subgraph of edge density at most ε or at least 1−ε
Rödl's proof uses the regularity lemma and gives a tower-type bound on 1/δ
Fox and Sudakov's bound δ ≥ 2^{-c|H|(log 1/ε)^2}, which implies Theorem 3.11
contents.reason: Their bound comes from a regularity-free proof built on an Erdős–Hajnal candidate-set lemma; recording the number without that proof would be an unsupported claim, and building the proof is a second route to the same theorem rather than part of this page's remit.

contents.name: Conjecture 3.12 (the polynomial Rödl conjecture)
contents.reason: Polynomial Rödl is one of the three equivalent properties in the Bucić–Fox–Pham theorem and the plan gives that equivalence its own page directly after this one.

contents.name: Problem 3.13 (asking for one part of the pair to be of linear size)
contents.reason: This asks for an asymmetric pure pair with one linear side, an open problem about pair densities rather than about a single restricted set, and no page in the plan claims it.

contents.name: Conjecture 3.14 (triangle-free graphs and disjoint sets of orders cn and n^c with no edges between them)
contents.reason: The triangle-free special case is a Ramsey-number statement about K3 against a complete bipartite graph and is open; recording it would state an unproved claim with no use on this page.

contents.name: Conjecture 3.15 (the multicolour generalisation)
contents.reason: Multicoloured complete graphs and their subcolourings are a Ramsey-colouring formalism the library has not introduced, and this page never colours edges.

contents.name: Fox, Grinshpun and Pach on rainbow-triangle-free three-colourings
contents.reason: This is a sharp result about three-edge-colourings and lexicographic products of colourings, which again needs the colouring formalism the library has not built.

contents.name: the tournament form of the conjecture and Berger, Choromanski and Chudnovsky's results
contents.reason: Tournaments are directed and the library develops only finite simple undirected graphs, so the transitive-subtournament statement cannot even be phrased at this point.

contents.name: Conjecture 3.16 and the hypergraph analogues
contents.reason: Three-uniform hypergraph Erdős–Hajnal needs hypergraph Ramsey and stepping-up constructions; the library has finite hypergraph definitions only inside extremal graph theory and no hypergraph Ramsey theory.

sources.title: J. Fox and B. Sudakov, Induced Ramsey-type theorems
sources.locator: §1 Background and Introduction, including §1.1, PDF pp. 1–7

contents.name: k-universal graphs and the function hom(G)
the Erdős–Szemerédi bound for graphs of small edge density
contents.reason: The Erdős–Szemerédi improvement of Erdős–Szekeres for sparse or dense graphs quantifies hom(G) against the density and belongs with the classical bounds rather than with the extraction of a restricted set.

contents.name: Rödl's theorem, stated as a linear-size induced subgraph with edge density at most ε or at least 1−ε
the statement of Szemerédi's regularity lemma and the definitions of edge density, ε-regular pair and equitable partition
Gowers's tower-type lower bound on M(ε), and the resulting weakness of the constant in Rödl's theorem
contents.reason: The tower-type lower bound on the number of parts is a construction of a graph forcing many parts; the published regularity page states only the upper bound, and no item here needs the matching lower bound.

contents.name: Theorem 1.1 (a regularity-free proof of Rödl's theorem with δ = 2^{-ck(log 1/ε)^2})
contents.reason: A second, regularity-free proof of Rödl's theorem with a far better constant is genuinely welcome, but it rests on the Erdős–Hajnal candidate-set lemma and a generalisation of the Graham–Rödl–Ruciński lemma, neither of which exists in the library at this order.

contents.name: Nikiforov's theorem: few induced copies of H force an equitable partition all of whose parts have density at most ε or at least 1−ε
contents.reason: Fox and Sudakov state Nikiforov's theorem in its stronger equitable-partition form, in which every part is sparse or dense; the greedy iteration that this page can supply leaves an uncovered remainder, so the partition form is not obtainable from the single-set theorem proved here.

contents.name: the Erdős–Hajnal theorem hom(G) ≥ 2^{c sqrt(log n)} for H-free graphs
contents.reason: Deriving the subexponential homogeneous-set bound from a restricted set requires the iteration that the classical-bounds page is built to carry, and this page deliberately avoids the invariant hom(G) entirely.

contents.name: Theorem 1.2 (a common strengthening of the Erdős–Hajnal and Promel–Rödl bounds)
contents.reason: The combined bound interpolates between universality and the homogeneous-set bound and is stated in terms of hom(G), which is not in this page's declared prerequisite closure.

contents.name: Theorem 1.3 (edge distribution: a half-size subset whose edge count deviates, answering Chung–Graham)
contents.reason: The deviation statement is about one prescribed subset of size n/2 rather than about a restricted subset of any size, and its proof route is the dependent-random-choice lemma, which is not available at this point in the reading order.

contents.name: §1.2 induced Ramsey numbers; Theorem 1.4, Corollary 1.5, Corollary 1.6 and Theorem 1.7
contents.reason: Induced Ramsey numbers and pseudo-random constructions for them are a Ramsey-theoretic subject with its own machinery; the library's Ramsey page has no induced Ramsey number and this page's results are not about colourings.

Theorem 1.1 (Rödl)
the polynomial Rödl property, and that it implies the Erdős-Hajnal property
contents.reason: The polynomial form asks for δ = ε^d uniformly in ε and its consequence for the conjecture is proved by taking ε polynomially small in the order; the plan gives that argument its own page.

Theorem 1.2 (Nikiforov)
viral families of graphs
